title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (continuing from the previous page). S has characteristic p, and X/S has relative dimension 1. Let F: X -> X^{(p)/S} be the relative Frobenius. Assume Ω^1_{X/S} is locally free of rank 1, i.e. X/S locally has a relative p-basis {x}. Let Λ be the image of O_{X^{(p)}} in F_*O_X, and set Q = F_*O_X/Λ. Q is locally free of rank p-1 over Λ, with basis the classes of x, x^2, ..., x^{p-1}. In the smooth case Q is the sheaf B_1 = F_*O_X/O_{X'} ≅ F_*O_X/O_{X'} --d--> F_*B^1 of locally exact differentials.

The pairing. In relative dimension 1 every relative 1-form is closed. So the Cartier operator C̃: F_*Ω^1_{X/S} -> Ω^1_{X^{(p)}/S}⊗Λ is defined on all 1-forms and kills exact forms. Grothendieck defines φ(f,g) = C̃(f dg).
(a) φ is Λ-bilinear, because C̃ is p^{-1}-linear and d(a^p g) = a^p dg.
(b) φ vanishes if f=1 or g=1, since dg is exact and d1 = 0. Hence φ descends to a pairing Q×Q -> Ω^1_{X^{(p)}/S}⊗Λ.
(c) φ is antisymmetric, because f dg + g df = d(fg) is exact. For p≠2 it is moreover alternating: f df = d(f^2/2). For p=2 it is symmetric but not alternating, since C(x dx) = dx'.

Proposition: the pairing is perfect. Proof: C̃(x^i d x^j) = j·C̃(x^{i+j-1}dx). This is nonzero, equal to j·dx', exactly when i+j-1 ≡ p-1, i.e. i+j = p. So the Gram matrix is anti-diagonal with entries p-1, ..., 2, 1. Its determinant is ±(p-1)! = ∓1 by Wilson's theorem (the marginal note gives Δ = -1 ∈ F_p^*), so it is invertible.

Corollary: there is a canonical isomorphism Q ≅ Q^∨ ⊗ (Ω^1_{X^{(p)}/S}⊗Λ). Taking determinants gives det Q ≅ det Q^∨ ⊗ ω'^{⊗(p-1)}⊗Λ. On the next page this becomes det(Q)^{⊗2} ≅ ω'^{⊗(p-1)}⊗Λ.

Purpose: to extract canonical square roots of (powers of) the relative canonical sheaf from Frobenius. For p=2, Q is a line bundle with Q^2 ≅ ω, giving a canonical theta characteristic. For p odd he hopes for a canonical det Q ≅ ω^{(p-1)/2} with no sign ambiguity. This sits inside his study of Cartier duality and the inverse Cartier operator for Gauss–Manin.
errors: The case condition is written 'i+j ≠ p-1 / i+j = p-1'. It should be i+j = p, since x^{i+j-1}dx contributes only when i+j-1 = p-1. The anti-diagonal matrix he draws (entries p-1, ..., 2, 1) is correct for i+j = p, so this is a slip of notation only.
He writes 'f dg + g df = d(fg) = 0'. d(fg) is not zero; what vanishes is C̃(d(fg)), because the form is exact. Again a slip.
The value of C̃(x^i dx^j) is j·dx' (dx' a basis of Ω^1_{X^{(p)}/S}), not the scalar j. This is harmless for the determinant argument.
Antisymmetry alone does not give 'alternating if p≠2'. One needs φ(f,f) = C̃(d(f^2)/2) = 0, which is immediate but not stated.

The determinant equals sign(antidiagonal permutation)·(p-1)!. He says 'au signe près', which is fine. The precise sign attempted on the next page should be checked: for p odd the form is alternating, so the determinant must be a square in F_p, consistent with ((p-1)/2)!^2 = (-1)^{(p+1)/2}.

ideas.what: Perfect pairing on B = F_*O_X/O_{X'} for a curve (or 1-dimensional p-basis situation) given by (f,g) ↦ C(f dg) with values in Ω^1_{X'}, so B ≅ B^∨⊗ω.
ideas.modern_name: Cartier-duality self-duality of the bundle of locally exact differentials B_1 (ω-valued symplectic for p odd, symmetric for p=2)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Raynaud, 'Sections des fibrés vectoriels sur une courbe' (1982); later used by Joshi, Mehta–Pauly and others

ideas.what: Computation of the Gram matrix in a p-basis as anti-diagonal (1, ..., p-1), with determinant ±(p-1)! = ∓1 by Wilson's theorem.
ideas.modern_name: Local computation of the Cartier pairing; Wilson's theorem

ideas.what: Consequence det(Q)^2 ≅ ω^{p-1}. For p=2 this makes ω canonically a square (canonical theta characteristic in characteristic 2), worked out on the next page.
ideas.modern_name: Canonical theta characteristic in characteristic 2 / det B ≅ ω^{(p-1)/2}
ideas.usually_credited_to: Mumford (Theta characteristics, 1971) for char 2 (I believe); Raynaud 1982 for det B

missed.claim: Grothendieck, apparently around 1972, set up the self-duality of B_1 = F_*O_X/O_{X'} via (f,g) ↦ C(f dg) in a relative setting. He works over a base S with only a one-element p-basis assumed (not necessarily smooth), with values in Ω^1_{X'/S}⊗Λ. This anticipates the structure Raynaud exploited in 1982. It is a priority/record detail rather than a new theorem.
missed.quote: Proposition L'accouplement (*) est une dualité parfaite de Λ-modules.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical credit only. The relative, possibly non-smooth formulation is mildly more general than usual textbook statements, but specialists would find nothing mathematically new.

missed.claim: The page shows the form is alternating for p odd, yet on the next page Grothendieck looks for the canonical sign of det Q ≅ ω^{(p-1)/2} via bases. The Pfaffian of the ω-valued symplectic form directly gives the canonical isomorphism det Q ≅ ω^{(p-1)/2}⊗Λ. He does not seem to make this link explicitly.
missed.quote: φ est antisymétrique, i.e. alterné si p≠2
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor: it resolves his stated μ_2 ambiguity. It is standard knowledge today.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is a clean, correct (modulo slips) derivation of the known self-duality of the sheaf of locally exact differentials via the Cartier operator, leading to the char-2 canonical theta characteristic. It is known in the literature (Raynaud 1982, Mumford-era char-2 theta characteristic), so it has only mild interest for dating and priority.
transcription_corrections: The marginal note reads 'Δ = -1 ∈ F_p^*' (Wilson), not just '= -1 ∈ F_p^*'.
The case condition is indeed written 'i+j ≠ p-1' / 'i+j = p-1' in the manuscript (author's slip; the correct condition is i+j = p).
'ℰ' under the corollary is likely a stray mark or bracket, not mathematical content.
The '[?]' after 'd(fg) = 0' can be dropped: the manuscript reads 'd(fg) = 0.'
